claim_boundary: Simplot announced a strawberry gene-editing alliance with PSI, pairing its CRISPR-Cas9 technology with PSI germplasm and commercialization expertise. Shelf-life and waste improvements were targets, not a reported launch.
Simplot announced agricultural research and commercial CRISPR-Cas9 licensing from Corteva and the Broad Institute. This IP agreement does not establish a marketed berry product.

Ohalo announced Boosted Breeding, a proprietary plant breeding system intended to transmit complete parental genomes. The company describes applications across potato, corn and berries; its performance statements are company claims.

Ohalo announced a strawberry consortium using its proprietary hybrid plant breeding system and uniform true seed. Field trials were expected in 2026; the announcement does not demonstrate that those trials or commercial sales occurred.

Ohalo describes its strawberry true-seed hybrid breeding consortium and intended flavor, propagation and sustainability benefits. Commercial availability and trial outcomes are not established by this undated program page.

Pairwise and PSI announced gene-editing collaboration on black and red raspberries and blackberries. Pairwise supplies editing, while PSI contributes germplasm and nursery expertise. Proposed traits include taste, convenience, shelf life and off-season availability.

Pairwise reports genome-edited compact blackberry outdoor trials in the US and Colombia and consumer sales in Colombia. Seedless blackberries are described separately as a greenhouse pipeline. Volumes, named retailers and independent field results are not disclosed.

Pairwise introduced Fontana, a compact fresh-market blackberry built on a PSG variety. The release makes company performance claims and describes thornless and seedless blackberries as future pipeline products, rather than as demonstrated Fontana traits.

Pairwise announced a seedless blackberry using CRISPR plant editing and described separate compact and thornless edits. The company defines seedless as soft small seeds rather than an absence of seeds. Future field testing and market availability were anticipated.

Pairwise and Hudson River Biotechnology announced a Fulcrum plant gene-editing license for incorporation into HRB editing services, including vegetables and soft fruit. The license does not identify a newly launched berry variety.

HRB and Plantik announced a strawberry heat-tolerance genome-editing collaboration combining Plantik targets with HRB transgene-free editing and BioMaas. The source says validation trials are underway; tomato demonstrations do not establish strawberry field performance.
HRB reports regeneration of strawberries from gene-edited single cells using its TiGER CRISPR workflow. This is an enabling-method demonstration, not evidence of a named commercial edited strawberry.

Plantik describes ATLANTIS target discovery in non-coding regulatory DNA and PROEDIT delivery of CRISPR machinery for plant genome editing. Its platform targets complex traits including heat tolerance; platform claims are not product approvals.

AgFunderNews reports the Plantik-HRB strawberry heat-tolerance partnership and distinguishes tomato validation from strawberry development. This provides reporting context, not independent replication of company performance claims.
HortiDaily covers the Plantik-HRB strawberry heat-tolerance partnership. Coverage derives from the same announced collaboration and is not counted as independent confirmation.
Fall Creek describes its commercial blueberry genetics and grower-support Collection platform and access to applied research trials. Gene editing is not established by this source.
Planasa describes berry breeding using traditional breeding methods and modern technology, supported by nursery operations. The page does not establish gene editing in a named Planasa program.

Heritable, CIV and Paul J. Mastronardi announced an AI-driven predictive breeding collaboration for greenhouse and tabletop strawberries, targeting taste, disease resistance and yield. The release does not establish CRISPR use in this strawberry program.

Qi Biodesign reports $75 million total financing and its SEEDIT plant genome-editing platform, including nucleases, base editors, prime editors and PrimeRoot. The release reports high-oleic soybean and disease-resistant wheat milestones; those regulatory assertions remain attributed to the company.
Vilmorin & Cie announced a global license to Qi Biodesign genome-editing technologies for field and vegetable crops, including access to a CRISPR nuclease. No berry-specific product is named.

A Beijing government science portal reports approval of a Qi Biodesign agricultural genome-editing laboratory and reports five safety certificates across soybean, wheat and rice. This article is not the original product-specific regulatory certificate.

KWS reports a worldwide plant-breeding gene-editing license from Shunfeng Bio covering Cas-SF01 and Cas-SF02 enzymes and all crop types. A global IP license is not global product approval or proof of a berry program.
German-language KWS coverage of the same Shunfeng genome-editing license. This is another language edition of the same publisher announcement and is not independent corroboration.

Defra published a marketing notice for Simplot S4A-210 strawberry and related lines, describing Tfl1 CRISPR/Cas9 edits and planned 2026 line-selection trials in England. The notice does not prove completed trials, retail sale or authorization in all jurisdictions.

An APHIS response dated August 6, 2020 concludes that the described Simplot remontant genome-edited strawberries are not regulated under the cited 7 CFR part 340 framework, based on representations and conditions in the inquiry. Other authorities may apply.

This APHIS-hosted document is Qi Biodesign’s high-oleic soybean regulatory-status-review request, revised May 23, 2024, describing FAD2 edits. It is an applicant submission, not itself an APHIS approval or determination letter.

APHIS determined that the specified high-oleic soybean with loss of seed-specific FAD2 function is not subject to 7 CFR part 340. This is a plant-pest regulatory determination, not an FDA decision, berry authorization or proof of sales.

The issuer announced PSG would hold berry breeding populations and related IP, while PSI would supply research and propagation under contract. Fifteen populations were described: eight strawberry, three blueberry, two raspberry, one blackberry and one black raspberry. Executed assignments, capitalization and Simplot agreement novation remain unresolved.

Ohalo announced a development and commercialization agreement with UF/IFAS, Florida Foundation Seed Producers and FSGA. It reports integrating a resistance trait into existing Florida strawberry varieties using proprietary advanced breeding. Non-commercial experimental trials were forecast for 2025; their completion, named releases and sales are not established.

The investor describes a small-berry gene-editing innovation center and industrialization initiative in Nanjing, linked to the Lishui blueberry industry and Joyvio-related growing, sales and processing. It dates an A+ investment exceeding RMB 100 million to May 2026 in its body text; the page publication date is unknown. No named edited-blueberry cultivar, completed trial or sale is established.

FDA lists voluntary premarket meetings for Simplot remontant strawberry and Pairwise blackberry traits. FDA explicitly distinguishes a meeting from its evaluation in a completed voluntary premarket consultation. Neither a meeting nor an inventory row proves sales.

FDA records a December 4, 2024 meeting for strawberry altered flowering and loss-of-function edits in confidential Gn1. The inventory identifies Simplot. This closes the missing FDA-record search, not food approval, commercial availability or an independent Gn1-to-TFL1 identity determination.

FDA records a July 9, 2026 blackberry meeting concerning compact architecture, reduced prickles and reduced seed lignification. The record does not identify Fontana, a sold cultivar, or a fully stacked commercial product. A VPM is not an FDA food-safety evaluation.

The voluntary non-novel list names Simplot S4A, CRISPR/Cas9, longer harvest season and anticipated marketing in 2025. Anticipated marketing is not an actual sale or a novel-food approval. The row alone does not map each English S4A subline.

The July 17, 2026 confirmation covers eight PBM/26/FRAN/008 identifiers; the government notice maps them to eight S4A lines. This is precision-bred status, separate from food authorization, completed England trials or sales.

MARA lists certificate 350 for Shandong Shunfeng GmELF3a soybean 25T93-1 and certificate 351 for Suzhou Qi GmFAD2-1A/GmFAD2-1B soybean P16. Both are nationwide production/application certificates valid January 2, 2024 through January 1, 2029. The list does not prove sales, berry authorization, or the Beijing/Suzhou ownership chain.

PSG describes its roots in PSI and a consolidation under the PSG name in 2024, while the 2023 issuer release announced restructuring. Its history reports Simplot investment in PSG. Neither source discloses ownership percentages, control, executed assignments or contract novation; announcement and implementation dates remain distinct.

PSG currently describes implementing gene editing with Pairwise across caneberry breeding programs and with Simplot in strawberry programs. This provides current partner-side corroboration of the historical alliances. It does not identify which specific S4A line derives from PSG germplasm or prove a commercial launch.

Heritable explicitly markets genome-edit design for CRISPR or targeted mutagenesis, off-target prediction and multi-gene optimization. These are company platform claims; the page does not establish use in its CIV/Mastronardi strawberry program, completed field validation, or a released edited strawberry.

Planasa describes biomolecular markers, molecular analysis, breeder phenotyping and crossing selected individuals. This supports marker-assisted breeding. No editing method or edited-berry launch is established by this page.

The UF 2024-25 report names Ohalo as a collaborator in a DNA-free editing system. It reports 138 regenerated lines across four varieties and 20 selected for 2025-26 field testing after growth-room assays. Methods name five cultivars while results enumerate four; no fifth result cohort is inferred. Field completion and commercial launch are not reported.

PubMed PMID 41635864 indexes a strawberry MYB10-1B CRISPR paper and lists Fall Creek as an author affiliation. Publication was October 15, 2025 with January 2026 collection. Affiliation alone does not establish a Fall Creek corporate editing program, a blueberry editor, ownership of results or an edited commercial product.

Company recruitment material hosted by China Agricultural University names Shandong Shunfeng Biotechnology and a bellagen.cn recruitment email. This establishes a domain association, not a separately incorporated BellaGen company or a legal renaming instrument.

HRB names Oost NL and Eurogenetic in a financing announcement, with Bridford Group and Elaine Groenestein as existing investors. Visible body date 04.09.2024 controls over shared site metadata. Investment amount and controlling ownership are not disclosed.

Planasa identifies itself as part of EW Group in the IFSI issuer announcement. Its page is dated May 12, 2026 and the body announcement May 6; those dates remain distinct. This closes the parent-identification source gap, without establishing berry gene editing.

A Simplot presentation hosted by SCRA describes S4A as CRISPR/Cas9 edited and uses the confidential target label Gn1. Its composition and environmental statements remain company assessments; the presentation is not an agency decision or proof of a specific retail SKU.
